passage:
In the school library, Ms Kaur noticed Payal sitting alone again, far from Vandana's table. Six months ago the two had been inseparable.
When Payal's phone buzzed, she flinched, read it and typed a reply fast. "Sorry, sorry," she whispered to no one.
Ms Kaur sat down beside her. "You've seemed worried lately. Want to talk?"
Payal hesitated, then it came out in pieces. Yuvraj didn't like Vandana. He got upset if Payal replied late, so she'd stopped going to Vandana's house. She felt guilty whenever she laughed with anyone else. "I keep saying sorry for things I didn't do," she said. "Maybe it's my fault."
"It's not your fault," Ms Kaur said quietly. "Caring about someone shouldn't make your world smaller. Thank you for telling me." She stayed with Payal until the bell, then walked her to the school counsellor's room that same afternoon, and Payal agreed to talk there.

qa.q: Why had Payal stopped going to Vandana's house?
qa.a: Yuvraj got upset if Payal replied late, so she stopped going to Vandana's house.

qa.q: What does Payal's constant 'sorry' suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Payal feels guilty for innocent things and is tiptoeing to avoid upsetting Yuvraj, even blaming herself.

qa.q: How did Ms Kaur respond in a wise way?
qa.a: Ms Kaur listened calmly, told Payal it wasn't her fault, stayed with her and took her to the school counsellor the same afternoon.

qa.q: What might Vandana be experiencing as Payal pulls away?
qa.a: Vandana may feel confused and hurt, losing a close friend without understanding why, and might even think Vandana did something wrong.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl feeling guilty for innocent things and dropping a friend to keep her boyfriend calm, and a teacher bringing in a trusted adult's view.

passage:
Dear Harsha didi,
I'm writing because I can't say this on the family group, and Mummy would panic.
You know Nakul. He's sweet, mostly. But lately I feel like I'm always in trouble without doing anything. If I don't reply in five minutes, he asks who I was with. When I went to Tanya's birthday, he didn't talk to me for two days, so I skipped the next party. I've stopped going to dance class because it finishes late and he gets "worried".
The strange part is that I feel guilty all the time, as if I'm the one who's wrong. I keep making myself smaller so he stays calm.
Is this normal? You're the only grown-up I trust not to laugh or shout. Could you call me on Sunday?
Love,
your little sister, Gargi

qa.q: Why has Gargi stopped going to dance class?
qa.a: Gargi stopped because it finishes late and Nakul gets 'worried'.

qa.q: Why does Gargi feel guilty even though she hasn't done anything wrong?
qa.a: Nakul's reactions have made Gargi feel always in trouble, so she blames herself and keeps shrinking her life to keep him calm.

qa.q: How could Harsha respond when calling Gargi on Sunday?
qa.a: Harsha could listen calmly, tell Gargi it isn't her fault, and on that call help her bring in a parent or school counsellor the same day, rather than waiting to see.

qa.q: How might Nakul see his own 'worry'?
qa.a: Nakul probably sees his worry as care, not realising it is making Gargi drop friends and dance to keep him calm.

grounding: Illustrates a teenage girl's strain in a controlling relationship, feeling guilty and giving up friends and dance, and reaching out to a trusted older cousin.

passage:
Masi,

Can I ask you something without you telling Mumma yet?

Eshaan and I have been together since March. He's sweet mostly. But he gets upset if I talk to boys, even in group projects. So I stopped sitting with Karan and Ali in physics, though we've been friends since Class 6.

Then he didn't like me going to Gunjan's sleepover, because her brother would be home. So I didn't go. I said I had a stomach ache.

Now I feel guilty for small things. If I laugh at someone's joke, I check Eshaan's face. I don't even know what I did wrong. I just feel like I'm always about to do something wrong.

Is this normal? Everyone says he loves me a lot.

Swati

Masi's reply, the same evening: Swati, thank you for telling me. Loving someone shouldn't mean your world gets smaller. Can I come over tomorrow after school? Nothing you did is wrong.

qa.q: Why did Swati skip Gunjan's sleepover?
qa.a: Because Eshaan didn't like her going, since Gunjan's brother would be home.

qa.q: How does Swati feel when she laughs at someone's joke?
qa.a: She feels guilty and anxious, checking Eshaan's face as if she is always about to do something wrong.

qa.q: Was writing to Masi a good step, and why?
qa.a: Yes; a trusted adult could help Swati see that loving someone should not mean shrinking her world, and Masi replied the same evening.

qa.q: What would change if Swati kept going without telling anyone?
qa.a: Her world might keep shrinking and she might lose more friends, feeling guilty for innocent things without any outside view.

grounding: Swati feels guilty for innocent things and drops friends to keep peace with Eshaan, then turns to her Masi, a trusted adult, for perspective.

passage:
You want to know what it felt like? I'm Nirmala. And the honest answer is, I didn't notice it happening.

Tanvir didn't like my friends. He never said "stop seeing them." He just sulked for hours when I went out with them. So I went out less. Then I stopped going to the art club, because a senior he didn't like was in it.

I felt guilty all the time. If my phone buzzed, my heart jumped, even if it was just my mother. I started saying sorry for things I hadn't done.

One evening my mother asked why I never drew anymore. I burst into tears and told her everything, right there in the kitchen.

She didn't shout. She held me and said, "Loving someone should not make your world smaller." That night she helped me list the things I'd given up. It was a long list.

The next day I went back to art club.

qa.q: What club did Nirmala stop going to?
qa.a: The art club.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when her phone buzzed?
qa.a: Her heart jumped with guilt and fear, even when it was just her mother.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She listened calmly the same evening, told Nirmala that love should not shrink her world, and helped her list what she had given up.

qa.q: What might Tanvir experience as Nirmala goes back to art club?
qa.a: He may feel threatened or upset, since his sulking had been keeping her world small.

grounding: Nirmala tiptoes around Tanvir and drops friends and art club to keep the peace, until her mother, a trusted adult, helps her see love should not shrink her world.

passage:
Monday. Noor told Sahil she was going to the library with Fiza after school. Sahil sulked all through lunch. "Why do you need Fiza? You have me." Noor felt guilty and cancelled.

Thursday, the following week. Noor didn't go to her cousin's birthday because Sahil said her cousin's friends were "too much." She told her cousin she had exams. She had no exams. Sitting at home, she felt small and oddly relieved: at least there would be no fight.

Saturday, a month on. Fiza stopped messaging. Noor realised she had dropped three friends since the term started. She checked Sahil's mood before she checked her own.

That evening her Khala noticed Noor staring at her phone at dinner. After dinner Khala took her onto the balcony. "You've gone very quiet. Tell me." Noor told her everything.

Khala listened, then said gently, "Loving someone should never mean shrinking your world. Tomorrow we'll call Fiza together."

qa.q: Who did Noor plan to go to the library with?
qa.a: Fiza.

qa.q: How did Noor feel sitting at home instead of at her cousin's birthday?
qa.a: She felt small, and also oddly relieved that there would be no fight, showing how much she was tiptoeing around Sahil.

qa.q: How did Khala respond, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Khala noticed, asked gently, listened, told Noor love should not shrink her world, and planned a concrete step with Fiza the next day.

qa.q: How might Fiza feel after Noor keeps cancelling?
qa.a: She probably feels hurt and pushed away, which is why she stopped messaging.

grounding: Over a month Noor feels guilty for innocent things and drops friends to keep Sahil calm, until her Khala, a trusted adult, helps her see it.

passage: Tarun, I'll tell you about my sister Lata. Your Darshan Dada was twenty then, she was fifteen, and she was seeing a boy in her class, Manoj. At first she glowed. Then she began saying sorry all the time: for a friend's birthday photo, for replying late, for laughing at someone else's joke. She stopped going to her friend Pooja's house on Saturdays because "Manoj gets upset." At dinner she checked her phone under the table with a small frightened face. One evening I found her crying on the stairs over a message from him, and she said, "It's my fault, I shouldn't have gone." Gone where? To her own cousin's wedding. I did not shout. I sat on the step beside her and asked, "Shall we talk to Amma together, now?" She nodded. We went that very night, and Amma listened without blaming Lata once. That was where she started finding her world again.

qa.q: What did Lata stop doing on Saturdays?
qa.a: She stopped going to her friend Pooja's house on Saturdays.

qa.q: What was Lata feeling when she said, 'It's my fault, I shouldn't have gone'?
qa.a: She felt guilty and frightened, blaming herself for going to her own cousin's wedding because it upset Manoj.

qa.q: What turning point did Darshan create on the stairs, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stayed calm, sat beside her and took her to Amma that same night, so a trusted adult could help her see the pattern without blame.

qa.q: How might Pooja have experienced Lata's absence on Saturdays?
qa.a: Pooja may have felt hurt or confused, losing time with her friend without knowing the reason was Manoj getting upset.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl who feels guilty for innocent things and drops friends to keep her partner calm, and a trusted adult brought in the same night.
